title: The Servant at the Fairy's
subtitle: A dog corrects a servant's instructions

learningObjectives.text: What does the servant agree to?
What happens to time in the fairy's house?

fairy.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
fairy.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
fairy.locator: THE SERVANT AT THE FAIRY'S.; THE SERVANT AT THE FAIRY'S., normalized characters 383-1279
fairy.excerpt: She gave her her morning's work to do, and said to her: "We are fairies. I must go from home, but your work is in the kitchen; smash the pitcher, break all the plates, pound the children, give them breakfast (by themselves), dirty their faces, and rumple their hair." [50] While she was at breakfast with the children, a little dog comes to her and says: "Tchau, tchau, tchow; I too, I want something." "Be off from here, silly little dog; I will give you a kick." But the dog did not go away; and at last she gave him something to eat--a little, not much. "And now," says he, "I will tell you what the mistress has told you to do. She told you to sweep the kitchen, to fill the pitcher, and to wash all the plates, and that if it is all well done she will give you the choice of a sack of charcoal or of a bag of gold; of a beautiful star on your forehead, or of a donkey's tail hanging from it.
fairy.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: Hired at the fair
narrativeBlocks.body: A girl (or a boy, in some tellings) is hired at the fair by a fine lady — wages good, work light — and taken to a house that turns out to be the fairy's.

narrativeBlocks.title: The one rule
narrativeBlocks.body: The service is easy and the wages rich — with one condition, always just one: don't look through the keyhole, don't ask who the visitors are, don't touch that one thing.

narrativeBlocks.title: The broken rule
narrativeBlocks.body: Of course the rule is broken — the servant looks, or asks, or touches — and the fairy's house vanishes or dismisses her. The service ends on the spot.

narrativeBlocks.title: Paid in full, years later
narrativeBlocks.body: She is paid her wages and sent home — but home is changed: years have passed for a single year's service. The fairy pays exactly — and keeps exactly — what was bargained.

narrativeBlocks.title: The Labourd fairy
narrativeBlocks.body: These aren't the ethereal fairies of romance: the Labourd fairy is a fine lady who hires fairly and dismisses instantly — a village tale about rules and the cost of curiosity.

quiz.prompt: What is the one rule of the fairy's service?

choices.text: Never leave the house at night
Don't look through the keyhole / don't ask / don't touch — a single forbidden act

quiz.explanation: One small rule — and the whole tale is about breaking it.

quiz.prompt: What happens when the servant goes home?

choices.text: Years have passed for a single year's service — time runs differently in the fairy's house

quiz.explanation: The fairy pays exactly what was bargained — in fairy-time.
